1.pericope_label: And there was given me a reed like unto a rod: and the angel stood, saying, Rise, and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and them that worship therein

schools.summary: Begin with the word: an old word for a growing reed such as grew in immense brakes in the Jordan valley, also a writer’s reed, and also a measuring-rod as in Ezekiel, which is the sense here; the rod it is likened to is properly a staff used for scourging, for leaning on in walking, or for a sceptre, and also of a measuring-pole, so that the comparison is one of size and convenience for handling. Then settle the text: the clause and the angel stood is wanting in many manuscripts and editions, is rejected by three named editors and marked doubtful by a fourth, and appears to have been introduced from Zechariah; the best critical authority is against it and the connection does not demand it, so we may take the meaning to be that whoever gave the reed also spoke the command. Add that the transaction is impersonal throughout: it is not said by whom the reed was given, nor who speaks. Distinguish next the two Greek words rendered temple, the one signifying the whole compass of the sacred enclosure with its outer courts, porches and porticoes, the other the house of God itself, the Holy and the Holy of Holies; when Christ is said to teach in the temple the first is used, but when Zacharias goes into the temple the second is used, since he left the people in the outer court. It is the second which stands here. Say that the measuring cannot be of the literal building, whether standing or not, since its dimensions were sufficiently well known; the temple must denote what it represents, the church, God’s dwelling on earth, so that the command is to take an accurate estimate of the true church as distinguished from all other bodies of men, such an estimate that its characteristics could be made known and transmitted. Take the altar in the same way: as the altar was the place of sacrifice, to measure it is to take an estimate of the church with reference to its views of the sacrifice for sin and the method of reconciliation with God. Or read the measuring as protection instead: it implies the token of a resolve to protect a portion of the sacred enclosure from desecration, and is a sign of preservation during impending dangers, as the sealing was in the earlier vision. Find the basis of the vision in the Old Testament, in the prophet brought to a high mountain who saw a man with a line of flax and a measuring line; but prefer the other prophet’s vision of the man with the measuring rod sent to measure Jerusalem, since that is followed two chapters later by the vision of the two olive trees, which are distinctly identified with the two witnesses of this chapter. And admit the difficulty honestly: modern scholars do not know how to interpret this interlude before the seventh trumpet, one taking it for a scrap from the Zealot party before the destruction of Jerusalem and another denying any possible literal interpretation and taking the language in a wholly eschatological sense; there are three points in it however understood, the chastisement of Jerusalem, the mission of the two witnesses, and the rescue of the remnant. Note also that this chapter is very improperly separated from the preceding and improperly ended, since it should have closed at the eighteenth verse, the last verse belonging to the chapter that follows.

Give the measures first: a measuring reed, which with the Jews was six cubits long and with the Greeks and Romans ten feet, and which one version here calls a golden reed. Say it was very likely given by the same angel who gave the little book, since he afterwards bids John arise and measure with it. Then take the reed itself for the holy Scripture, the word of God, which is elsewhere called a line, a rule and a rod, and which is the rule and measure of doctrine and faith, so that by it all doctrine is to be tried and measured and whatever is not agreeable to it is to be rejected; and it is equally the rule and measure of all discipline, worship and practice, laying down the plan of a gospel church, which should be gathered out of the world and separated from it, showing who are the proper materials of such a church, what officers are to be constituted in it, and what ordinances administered.

Refer the passage plainly to the prophet’s vision of the measured temple, and admit that how to understand either the one or the other is not so easy. In the former case the design of measuring seems to have been the rebuilding of the temple, and that with advantage; here the design seems to be either the preservation of it in the times of public danger and calamity that are foretold, or its trial, that it may be seen how far it agrees with the standard or pattern in the mount, or its reformation, that what is redundant, deficient or changed may be regulated according to the true model. Then observe how much was to be measured. First the temple, that is the gospel church in general, whether it be so built and so constituted as the gospel rule directs, whether it be too narrow or too large, the door too wide or too strait. Second the altar, which as the place of the most solemn acts of worship may stand for religious worship in general: whether the church has the true altars, both as to substance and situation — as to substance, whether they take Christ for their altar and lay down all their offerings there, and as to situation, whether the altar be in the holiest, that is, whether they worship God in spirit and in truth. Third the worshippers must be measured too, whether they make God’s glory their end and his word their rule in all their acts of worship, whether they come to God with suitable affections, and whether their conversation be as becomes the gospel.

Give the chapter its argument in brief — the command to measure the temple, the two witnesses who should prophesy twelve hundred and sixty days, their description, power and influence, their death by the beast from the bottomless pit, their rising after three days and a half and ascent to heaven, the great earthquake, the introduction to the third woe, and the sounding of the seventh angel. Then refer the reed to the prophet’s measuring line. And on the temple of God, take it strictly: this must refer to the temple of Jerusalem, and this is another presumptive evidence that it was yet standing when the book was written.

Take the reed to be the Apocalypse itself, which he subsequently exhibited to the churches; for the Gospel of the complete faith he wrote afterwards for the sake of our salvation, since when Valentinus and Cerinthus and Ebion and others of the school of Satan were scattered abroad throughout the world, there assembled to him from the neighbouring provinces all the bishops, and compelled him himself also to draw up his testimony. Then say that the measure of God’s temple is the command of God to confess the Father Almighty, and that His Son Christ was begotten by the Father before the beginning of the world and was made man in very soul and flesh, both of them having overcome misery and death; and that, received with His body into heaven by the Father, He shed forth the Holy Spirit, the gift and pledge of immortality; that He was announced by the prophets and described by the law, God’s hand and the Word of the Father, Lord over all and founder of the world. This is the reed and the measure of faith, and no one worships the holy altar save he who confesses this faith. Or else take the reed for the office of writing the Gospel, which is not useless with a vain lustre but is like the rod of equity, the rod of the kingdom of God, for it describes the eternal kingdom of Christ; and explain the command to rise, not that John was seated, but that the hearts of all are aroused by this word to measure the writings and actions of the Gospel, for then they find what progress they each one make, and how far they agree with the divine rule. Add that not all who are seen in the temple worship, and that the command is that a part should not be reckoned.

debates: Whether the temple measured is the building at Jerusalem or the church.
Whether the clause and the angel stood belongs in the text.
Whether the measuring means protection or assessment.
Which Old Testament measuring vision lies behind this one.
What the reed itself signifies.
outliers: Clarke alone takes the temple literally and uses it to argue that the book was written before the fall of Jerusalem.
Ellicott settles which temple is meant from the difference between two Greek words, illustrated from the Gospels.
Ellicott prefers Zechariah to Ezekiel as the background because Zechariah supplies the two olive trees as well.
Robertson admits outright that modern scholars do not know how to interpret the interlude, and names two incompatible readings.
Victorinus reports that the neighbouring bishops compelled John to write his Gospel against Valentinus, Cerinthus and Ebion.
Victorinus turns the measure of the temple into a creed, and makes confession of it the condition of worship at the altar.
Bede reads the command to rise as addressed to the reader rather than to John, who was not seated.

2.pericope_label: But the court which is without the temple leave out, and measure it not; for it is given unto the Gentiles: and the holy city shall they tread under foot forty and two months

schools.summary: Insist first that the rendering is too weak. The word implies more than a passing by or omission, usually carrying the idea of force or impulse, so that John was to do some decisive or positive act indicating that this was no part of the true temple — not merely not to include it in the measurement. Render it cast out, or cast without, and say the outer court is left to its fate. Identify it as the court of the Gentiles, the outer court to which Gentiles had access and within which they were not permitted to go; to an observer this would seem a part of the temple and those assembled there a portion of the true worshippers, but it was necessarily neither, since by Hebrew notions only those with the privilege of access to the inner court and the altar were reckoned true worshippers. Fill in the architecture: in Herod’s temple the outer court was marked off from the inner by the middle wall of partition, beyond which a Gentile could not go, and in that outer court was a house of prayer for the Gentiles — which is now cast out and given to the Gentiles in quite another sense, to be profaned by them. Or take the court to mean all that lies outside the sanctuary, and read the passage of the Church: our Lord had said that Jerusalem should be trodden down of the Gentiles, and the seer catches the thought and the deeper significance, for there is a treading down worse than the conqueror’s, when the world-power in men tramples the pearls of grace under foot like swine and turns fiercely on those who gave them. Such an experience the Church must undergo; the shrine shall be safe, but the spirit of the nations, though nominally Christian, will be the spirit of worldliness and even of violence, and in the outer court of church life there will be the ebbing and flowing mass who sit in the way of knowledge, stand idle in the market-place, and have no oil in their lamps. But there is a limit to the desecration. Set out the period in its three forms as they occur through the book: forty-two months here and again later, twelve hundred and sixty days twice, and a time and times and half a time; and trace the same period to Daniel. Note that the verb for treading means to trample with contempt, and that one commentator holds only the heavenly city can be called holy here, because of the Sodom and Egypt of a later verse, though the language may be merely symbolical.

Trace the allusion to the court of the Israelites, where was the great crowd and company of worshippers, the national church of the Jews, called by the prophet the outer court, and which he did measure, though this seer is forbidden to. Then be precise about whom it stands for. It does not design the visible church apostatised as succeeding the pure and apostolical church, nor the apostate church of Rome, antichrist and his followers, for these are meant by the Gentiles to whom the outward court is given. The worshippers in this outward court are a distinct set from the internal worshippers, the priests of God in the temple and at the altar and in the inner court, and distinct also from the Gentiles, the Papists; and they are no other than carnal Protestants, the bulk of the reformed churches, who have only the name but not the nature of living Christians, who have a form of godliness but deny its power, who are Jews outwardly but not inwardly, and who worship only in an external manner, attending to outward forms and ceremonies while knowing nothing of true doctrine, pure worship or spiritual religion.

Read the measuring as pointing to the approaching destruction of the temple and the termination of the whole Levitical service, and say this was to be done by the Gentiles, that is the Romans, who were to tread it down forty-two months, that is just three years and a half or twelve hundred and sixty days — and add that this must be a symbolical period. Or else refuse the symbolic reading and count plainly. The old temple had a court in the open air for the heathens who worshipped the God of Israel; cast it out of thy account and measure it not, as not being holy in so high a degree. Take treading to mean inhabiting, and the holy city to be Jerusalem: so they began to do before this was written, and it has been trodden almost ever since by the Romans, Persians, Saracens and Turks. But say that the severe kind of treading here peculiarly spoken of will not be until the trumpet of the seventh angel, toward the end of the troublous times; that it will continue only forty-two common months, or twelve hundred and sixty common days; and that this is but a small part of the larger reckoning.

debates: Whom the outer court represents.
Whether the forty-two months are a symbolic or a literal period.
Whether the holy city is Jerusalem, the Church, or the heavenly city.
How strong the command about the outer court is.
Whether the treading down is past, present or still future.
outliers: Gill identifies the outer court not with Rome but with carnal Protestants, the bulk of the reformed churches.
Ellicott applies it to nominal Christendom and says the spirit of the nations will be worldly though nominally Christian.
Wesley alone insists the months are common months and places the severe treading still in the future.
Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson independently judge the English leave out too weak for the Greek.
Robertson notes the irony that the court once given to Gentiles for prayer is now given to them to profane.
Ellicott finds in the treading a worse desecration than a conqueror’s, drawing on the saying about pearls and swine.
Robertson reports a commentator who restricts the holy city here to the heavenly Jerusalem.

3.pericope_label: And I will give power unto my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy a thousand two hundred and threescore days, clothed in sackcloth

schools.summary: Note first that the word power is not in the original, which reads simply I will give; some word like power, privilege, opportunity or boldness must be supplied to complete the sense, and the meaning is not that he would send two witnesses to prophesy, but that these were in fact such witnesses and that he would during that time permit them to exercise their prophetic gift. Say the number two denotes that the number would be small, and that it is not necessary to confine it literally to two persons or two societies, since under the law two witnesses were required and were enough to establish any fact. On the identity, admit the article seems to point to two well-known characters, but that there is no possible way to determine who they are, and that all sorts of identifications have been attempted; the speaker may be God, or Christ, or an angel representative, and the construction that follows is Hebraic rather than the usual Greek idiom. Then ask instead why two: two witnesses were required for competent evidence, and there has constantly been a sending forth of God’s chosen messengers in pairs — Moses and Aaron, Elijah and Elisha, Joshua and Zerubbabel, and in New Testament times the disciples sent out two and two, and afterwards Paul with Barnabas and Paul with Silas. Beyond the mere mutual support that two can give, there is need for the association of two different characters in the same work: the energy and the sympathy, the elucidator of doctrines and the messenger to the conscience, the apologist and the evangelist, the man of thought and the man of action, the Son of Thunder and the Son of Consolation; it is well that in a world-wide work this duality of power should be brought into play. Insist that the word prophesy must be allowed a much wider meaning than merely to predict or foretell, since the compass of their work as afterwards described embraces much more: they work wonders recalling the days of Moses and Aaron, their words are mighty, and their life is a testimony. Note the period is symbolical but corresponds to that during which other witnesses had witnessed for God. On the participle for clothed, report that the chief manuscripts differ between accusative and nominative, that one editor suggests a mere slip and another a primitive error in the early copies for a dative agreeing with witnesses; and say simply that the dress suited the message.

Clear the ground by rejecting two identifications. These are not Enoch and Elias, as some of the ancient fathers thought, who supposed they would come before the appearance of Christ, oppose antichrist and be slain by him — a sense the Papists greedily catch at. Nor are the Scriptures meant, the two Testaments, Old and New, though their name and number agree and also their office, which is to testify of Christ; for to be clothed in sackcloth, to be killed, to rise again and to ascend to heaven are things that cannot well be accommodated to them. These witnesses rather intend the ministers of the gospel and the churches of Christ, who have borne testimony for Christ and against antichrist ever since he appeared in the world; and particularly the churches and ministers in Piedmont bid fair for this character, who were upon the spot when antichrist arose, always bore their protest against him, were ever independent of the church of Rome, subsisted in the midst of the darkness of the apostasy, suffered very great persecutions from the Papists, stood their ground, and continue to this day.

Observe that in this time of treading down God has reserved to himself his faithful witnesses, who will not fail to attest the truth of his word and worship. Consider the number: it is small, and yet sufficient. Small, because many will own and acknowledge Christ in times of prosperity who will desert and deny him in times of persecution, and one witness when the cause is upon trial is worth many at other times. Sufficient, because in the mouth of two witnesses every cause shall be established, and Christ sent out his disciples two by two to preach the gospel. Some think these two are Enoch and Elias, who are to return to the earth for a time; others, the church of the believing Jews and that of the Gentiles; it should rather seem that they are God’s eminent faithful ministers, who shall not only continue to profess the Christian religion but to preach it in the worst of times. Consider the time of their prophesying, which many take to be the period of the reign of antichrist; and if the beginning of that interval could be ascertained, this number of prophetic days, taking a day for a year, would give us a prospect when the end shall be. And consider their habit and posture: they prophesy in sackcloth, as those deeply affected with the low and distressed state of the churches and the interest of Christ in the world.

Say plainly that this is extremely obscure, that the conjectures of interpreters are as unsatisfactory as they are endless, and quote the judgment that they build conjectures upon conjectures with little likelihood, whose opinions it is not your business to rehearse; add that those who wish to be amused or bewildered may have recourse both to ancients and moderns on the subject. Elsewhere venture only this much: these seem to be two prophets, two select and eminent instruments, and the supposition that they are Moses and Elijah, whom they resemble in several respects, is without foundation. Take the days as common days, that is a hundred and eighty weeks, and say that so long will they prophesy, even while that last and sharp treading of the holy city continues, both by word and deed, witnessing that Jesus is the Son of God and the heir of all things, and exhorting all men to repent and fear and glorify God. And take the sackcloth for the habit of the deepest mourners, worn out of sorrow and concern for the people.

Say that the Lord, knowing the greatness of the adversary, grants indulgence to the godly, bidding those in Judaea flee to the mountains; but if any man is conscious that he is very stout-hearted to encounter Satan, let him stand, for you do not despair of the nerves of the Church, and let him say, Who shall separate us from the love of Christ. Let those who are fearful provide for their own safety, and those of good courage stand fast, for then shall be great tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world. But give thanks to God, who has confined the greatness of that tribulation to a few days, since for the elect’s sake those days shall be shortened, and Antichrist shall reign three years and a half only. And be careful about the authority: say we speak not from apocryphal books but from Daniel, who says they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time; and begin to reckon, a time being the one year.

debates: Who the two witnesses are.
Whether the number two is literal or a mark that the number is small.
Whether the days are prophetic days standing for years or common days.
Whether prophesying here means predicting or witnessing more widely.
On what authority the three and a half years is reckoned.
outliers: Clarke declines the question outright and tells the reader the literature is only amusing or bewildering.
Robertson agrees there is no possible way to determine who the witnesses are.
Gill rejects Enoch and Elias and the two Testaments, and names the churches of Piedmont as the likeliest fulfilment.
Ellicott abandons identification and asks instead why the messengers are sent in pairs, answering from the complementarity of characters.
Barnes and Ellicott both note the word power is absent from the Greek.
Cyril of Jerusalem refuses to argue from apocryphal books and takes the period from Daniel alone.
Henry proposes a day-for-a-year reckoning that would date the end if the start were known.

4.pericope_label: These are the two olive trees, and the two candlesticks standing before the God of the earth — and if any man will hurt them, fire proceedeth out of their mouth, and devoureth their enemies — these have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy, and have power over waters to turn them to blood, and to smite the earth with all plagues, as often as they will

schools.summary: Set out the prophet’s vision in full: a candlestick all of gold with a bowl on the top and seven lamps and seven pipes to the lamps, and two olive trees by it, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on the left, which are afterwards declared to be the two anointed ones that stand by the Lord of the whole earth. The olive trees appear connected with the ever-burning lamp by golden pipes, and as the olive tree produced the oil used by the ancients in their lamps, they represent a constant supply of oil to the candlestick, and so become emblematic of the supply of grace to the church. But say the seer does not use the emblem exactly in the prophet’s sense: there the lampstand is Israel and the olive trees are apparently the governor and the high priest, while here the two olive trees and the candlesticks are identical. Take the explanation to be deliberately general: the anointed ones are supposed to be those two men, or as others think the two prophets of that time; but the answer of the angel is general, and the vision age-long, reminding us of the returned exiles and of those who were then among them as anointed witnesses, while showing that such witnesses are to be found in more than one era — for those two cannot exhaust the fulness of a vision which represents the eternal truth that the oil of gladness and strength from God rests on those who rely, not on might or power, but on God’s Spirit. On the following powers, note the Old Testament basis throughout: the fire devouring their foes alludes to the fire called down on the captains, the closing of heaven to the drought, and the turning of water into blood and the summoning of plagues to Egypt; and note that the drought lasted three years and a half, just the period named here. But do not forget what has gone before: the witnesses are olive trees and lights, in whom grace, light and power are concentrated, and they wield a power which it is not safe to provoke. Refuse the literal reading of the fire: the meaning is that they would have the power of destroying their enemies as if fire proceeded from their mouth, their words being like burning coals. Explain the shut heaven from the ancient opinion that rain was kept in the clouds as in reservoirs or bottles, citing what is said of binding up the waters in thick clouds and of staying the bottles of heaven, so that to shut the heavens is to produce a drought; and allow that this may mean only that they were clothed with power to cause blessings to be withheld. Then press two points of grammar: the word rendered will is more than the sign of the future and denotes intention or purpose, if any man wills to injure them, and the word for hurt covers wrong in any form, whether to character, opinion, person or property; and note that it is impossible to hurt these two witnesses till they have done their work, that the condition is repeated the second time in a changed form as less likely to happen, and that death is then made inevitable.

Take the olive trees of the prophet’s vision to design the governor and the high priest, who in laying out themselves, their gifts and their wealth in rebuilding and finishing the temple were types of these witnesses, the ministers of the gospel in the successive ages of the apostasy. Say they may be compared to olive trees because of the oil of grace and the truth of it in them; because of the gifts of the Spirit bestowed on them, or that anointing which teacheth all things; because they freely impart their gifts and the golden oil of the gospel to others, and bring the good tidings of peace and salvation, of which the olive leaf is a symbol; and because they are like the olive tree, fat, flourishing and fruitful in spiritual things, sons of oil and God’s anointed ones. Then widen the hurting as far as it will go: doing any injury to their persons or properties, opposing their writings, blaspheming their doctrines, hindering their ministrations, whoever they be, whether living among them or in other parts, whether secret or open enemies, whether of the outward court or really Gentiles or Papists, and especially if they wrong, oppress, afflict and distress them knowingly and willingly. And on the power to shut heaven, say these have the keys of the kingdom given them, so that whatever they bind or loose on earth is bound or loosed in heaven — having the true key of knowledge in matters both of doctrine and discipline, whatever they declare according to the word of God to be fit to be received or rejected should be so.

Refer the emblem to the prophet, where the two olive trees represent the governor and the high priest, and say the whole account seems taken from that chapter; then admit honestly that whether the prophet and the apostle mean the same things by these emblems, we know not. Elsewhere carry the type forward: as those two were then the chosen instruments in God’s hand, even so shall these be in their season, and being themselves full of the unction of the Holy One they shall continually transmit the same to others; call them burning and shining lights, and take their standing before the Lord of the earth as always waiting on God, without the help of man, and asserting his right over the earth and all things therein. On the fire, say they are commissioned to denounce the judgments of God against all who would prevent them from proceeding in their ministry, and that whoever would kill them, as the Israelites would have done to Moses and Aaron, must be killed by that devouring fire. Trace the shut heaven to the prophet who shut it, and the blood and plagues to the lawgiver who afflicted Egypt. Then take the last clause as decisive of the question of identity: to smite the earth with all plagues, as often as they will, is not said of Moses, nor of Elijah, nor of any mere man besides — and ask how it is possible to understand this otherwise than of two individual persons. And locate the waters, taking them to be those in and near Jerusalem.

debates: Whether the seer uses the olive trees in the prophet’s sense or his own.
Whether the two witnesses are two individuals or a succession of ministers.
Whether the fire from their mouths is literal or figurative.
Whom the two anointed ones of the prophet were.
What the power to shut heaven amounts to.
outliers: Wesley argues from the plagues clause that the witnesses must be two individual persons, against every corporate reading.
Clarke admits he does not know whether prophet and apostle mean the same thing by the emblem.
Ellicott makes the generality of the angel’s answer the point, so that no single pair can exhaust the vision.
Robertson notes the seer collapses the prophet’s distinction, making trees and candlesticks identical.
Barnes explains the shut heaven from an ancient belief that rain was stored in the clouds like bottles.
Robertson observes it is impossible to hurt the witnesses until their work is done.
Gill turns the power to shut heaven into the power of the keys, over doctrine and discipline.

7.pericope_label: And when they shall have finished their testimony, the beast that ascendeth out of the bottomless pit shall make war against them, and shall overcome them, and kill them — and their dead bodies shall lie in the street of the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also our Lord was crucified — and they of the people and kindreds and tongues and nations shall see their dead bodies three days and an half, and shall not suffer their dead bodies to be put in graves

schools.summary: Take the verb rendered shall have finished in the sense of accomplishing rather than merely of time, and distinguish the two uses with examples from elsewhere. Say that only when their work is done has the wild beast power over them: to every one there are the symbolical twelve hours in which his life’s work must be achieved, and to every one the time is secured in which he may accomplish what God sent him to fulfil; then, but not till then, cometh the night when none can work. Of the beast, say he rises out of the abyss as the locust horde did, that we shall hear much of him later, and that here he is seen as a spirit of irreconcilable antagonism to Christ; the image is not new, the prophet having used it in a much more limited sense. Say nothing less than antichrist will satisfy the picture, note that some see Nero, and then decline to apply the prophecy to specific individuals or times, agreeing rather that the words cover in effect all the martyrdoms and massacres of history in which brute force has seemed to triumph over truth and righteousness. On the corpses, note there is no word for lie in the Greek, only their corpse upon the broad way, and that the noun wavers between singular and plural; explain the force of the image from antiquity, since nothing was reckoned more dishonourable than to leave a body unburied, and the Jews held it a special indignity, so that the meaning is that they would be treated with contempt for the time named. On the great city, take it clearly for Jerusalem in view of the closing clause about where their Lord was crucified, though it is not here called the holy city and though elsewhere in this book the great city is Babylon; note that the relative means which very city, and that the adverb rendered spiritually is used only twice in the New Testament, here in a hidden or allegorical sense. On the spectators, supply the word men before the partitive preposition; expect an assemblage of different classes such as would gather in a capital or a commercial city; and take the three days and a half either literally or, more in accordance with the style of this book, as prophetic days standing for years. Or else observe that the days of the gloating are as many as the years of the prophesying, but that there is no necessary correspondence of a day for a year; and describe the delight of the spectators as at once fiendish and childish.

Divide the finishing of the testimony from the prophesying. Their open public testimony as witnesses, so as to be heard and received, will be finished before the last war of the beast against them in which they will be killed; but their prophesying will continue to the end of the beast’s reign, these two being contemporary and of equal date, beginning and ending together — for they will prophesy when they are dead, being dead they will yet speak, and their very death will be a prophesying that the ruin of antichrist is at hand, which upon their resurrection and ascension will immediately come on. On the great city, deny that Jerusalem is meant: it was destroyed when this vision was given and will not be rebuilt at the time referred to, nor is it ever called the great city in this book, though the new Jerusalem is so called and that can never be designed here. Take it rather for the city of Rome, or the Roman jurisdiction, the whole empire of the Romish antichrist, which is often called the great city in this book; the city itself was very large and the empire still larger, so as to be called the whole world. And since the street of a city denotes a public open place, a place of concourse and resort, their bodies lying there may design the publicness of their silence, disgrace and contempt, so that the silencing and degrading of them will be known all over the antichristian empire.

Call the beast what is named antichrist, some power opposed to genuine Christianity; but confess that what it is, or whence, except from the bottomless pit, that is under the influence and appointment of the devil, we cannot tell, nor do we know by what name this power should be called. Then lay out the possibilities without choosing: if the whole passage refers to the persecution raised by the Jews against the Christians, then some Jewish power or person is the beast; if to the early ages of Christianity, then the beast may be one of the persecuting heathen emperors; if to a later age, then the beast may be the papal power, and the Albigenses and Waldenses the two witnesses, who were nearly extinguished by the horrible persecutions raised against them by the Church of Rome. Add that whatever may be intended, the earth has not yet covered their blood. On the great city, say some take it for Rome, which may be spiritually called Sodom for its abominations, Egypt for its tyrannous cruelty, and the place where our Lord was crucified because of its persecution of the members of Christ; but that Jerusalem itself may be intended, and that all these things must be left to others. Or take Jerusalem outright, a far greater city than any other in those parts, called Sodom and Egypt because the same abominations abound there at the time of the witnesses as once in Egypt and Sodom; and read the last clause historically, of the very ground where the cross stood, which was enclosed within the walls by Constantine, so that perhaps on that very spot will their bodies be exposed. On the refusal of burial, say they shall be treated with the greatest barbarity, since refusal of burial to the dead was allowed to be the sum of brutality and cruelty — and observe that in popish lands they will not suffer a Protestant to have Christian burial or a grave in a churchyard. And on the three days and a half, calculate: if we suppose this time began in the evening and ended in the morning, and included Friday, Saturday and Sunday, the weekly festival of the Turkish people, the Jewish tribes and the Christian tongues, then all these together, with the heathen nations, would have full leisure to gaze upon them and rejoice.

debates: Whether the great city is Rome or Jerusalem.
Who or what the beast from the bottomless pit is.
Whether the three days and a half are literal days or prophetic years.
Whether the finishing of the testimony and the end of the prophesying are the same moment.
Whether the passage can be applied to any particular persecution.
outliers: Gill denies the great city can be Jerusalem; Robertson calls it clearly Jerusalem on the strength of the same verse.
Clarke sets out three incompatible identifications of the beast and declines to choose among them.
Wesley locates the exposure of the bodies on the very ground of the crucifixion, enclosed by Constantine within the walls.
Robertson denies the day-for-a-year correspondence that Barnes allows, though he notes the numbers match.
Wesley reckons the three days to cover the weekly festivals of Turk, Jew and Christian at once.
Ellicott turns the beast’s delay into a general law, that every man has his twelve hours before the night comes.
Clarke uses the refusal of burial to attack the denial of Christian burial to Protestants in his own day.

10.pericope_label: And they that dwell upon the earth shall rejoice over them, and make merry, and shall send gifts one to another, because these two prophets tormented them — and after three days and an half the Spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet — and they heard a great voice from heaven saying unto them, Come up hither: and they ascended up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies beheld them

schools.summary: Narrow the word earth first: we now attach to it an idea not necessarily implied in the Hebrew or the Greek, and our word land would better express what is meant, so that the dwellers in the country where these things happen are the ones who rejoice. Say that while alive the witnesses would by their faithful testimony against existing errors excite so much hatred, and be so great an annoyance to the governing powers, that there would be general exultation when their voice was silenced — a thing so common in the world that there is no difficulty in applying the language. Or call the phrase for those who dwell on the earth an apocalyptic formula for the non-Christian world, describe the jubilant jollification over the cessation of the two prophets’ activity, and observe that such a sense of relief is perhaps not seldom felt today when a preacher of righteousness is removed. Trace the exchange of gifts to the Jewish feast where gifts were sent to one another and portions given to the poor. On the revival, note the phrase for the breath of life is used elsewhere of the lower animals, but that here there is clearly an allusion to the valley of dry bones, from which the very words they stood upon their feet are taken; note the tense changes from future to aorist as the prophecy becomes fact, and that the spectators were panic-stricken. Add the nearer memory of the three days of the Master’s death-sleep, and the promise that where he is there shall his servant be also; and draw the rule, that there is a resurrection power in even rejected truth, whose strength is undying, so that if it be of God men cannot overthrow it, and the cause that seemed dead is found possessed of renewed life — as when the orator of a council at Rome in 1514 cried that there was an end of resistance to the papal rule and that opposers existed no more, and within three years and a half the theses were nailed up at Wittenberg. On the voice, report that the manuscript authority is divided between they heard and I heard, the balance inclining to the former though the latter is what the seer writes two dozen times elsewhere. Insist that none of the ascent need occur literally, the whole being manifestly symbol: the meaning is that they would triumph as if they ascended to heaven and were received into the presence of God, and that it would be done openly, so that the enemies who had put them to death would see they were approved of God. Or take the ascension as the token that in this too they have a portion with their Lord, rejected and slain but welcomed and honoured, resting from their labours; and mark the one difference from the prophet taken up of old, that this is not done in comparative secret, for their enemies see their exaltation, the cause which seemed dead revives, and the martyred become glorious in the eyes of men — persecution dragging them into fame and chasing them up to heaven. Note also that the ascension of Christ was witnessed only by a few friends.

Identify those who dwell on the earth as the inhabitants of the Roman empire, often in this book called the earth, out of which the beast arose and over which he reigns, the followers of antichrist, men that mind nothing but earth and earthly things. On the interval, say the three days and a half are three years and a half, and that the delay is until it was certain they were dead and all hope of reviving was over. And on the voice, report that one printed edition with two of the versions reads I heard, that is John, though the copies in general read they, meaning not the enemies but the witnesses; and say the voice seems to come not from any Christian civil magistrate in the church but from Christ himself — not but that Christ may make use of such for bringing his people into a more glorious and comfortable state in this world.

Take those who dwell on the earth to denote earthly-minded men in particular; say they shall make merry as the Philistines did over Samson, and that the gifts will be sent to one another by Turks and Jews and heathens and false Christians alike. Note that sending gifts was a custom in days of public rejoicing, when men sent gifts to each other and gave portions to the poor. On the revival, say only that they were restored to their primitive state; and on the ascent, that they enjoyed a state of great peace and happiness. Take the voice as designed for all to hear; and observe that the enemies beheld them going up, who had not taken notice of their rising again, by which some had been convinced before.

debates: Whether the text reads they heard or I heard.
Whether the ascension is literal or symbolic.
Who is meant by those that dwell upon the earth.
What Old Testament passage stands behind the revival.
Whether the three days and a half here are days or years.
outliers: Four commentators independently weigh the same one-word variant and reach three different verdicts.
Ellicott dates a fulfilment to the month, setting a papal orator’s boast of 1514 against Luther’s theses three and a half years later.
Barnes insists the whole ascent is symbol and spells out what the symbol stands for.
Ellicott and Robertson both note the enemies witness this ascension, unlike the ascensions of Elijah and of Christ.
Robertson remarks that relief at the silencing of a preacher of righteousness is still felt today.
Barnes argues from a list of Old Testament and Gospel usages that earth here means only the land in question.
Wesley observes that the enemies had missed the resurrection and saw only the ascension.

13.pericope_label: And the same hour was there a great earthquake, and the tenth part of the city fell, and in the earthquake were slain of men seven thousand: and the remnant were affrighted, and gave glory to the God of heaven — the second woe is past; and, behold, the third woe cometh quickly

schools.summary: Take the earthquake as a symbol of commotion, agitation and change, of great political revolutions, and note that earthquakes are often given as a symbol of great upheavals in the social and spiritual order. Say the triumph of the witnesses would be followed by such revolutions as an earthquake would fitly represent; that the tenth part of the city means the tenth part of what the city represents, the persecuting power, the word tenth being used generally to denote that a considerable portion of that power would be involved in ruin; and that the seven thousand seems suggested because it would bear some proportion to a tenth part, so that no literal count need be sought. Note that only a tenth falls here, where a third fell under the earlier trumpets, perhaps a conventional number; that the Greek says names of men, an idiom found in the papyri and elsewhere in this book; and that the phrase for affrighted means became terrified. Ask whether it is accidental that seven thousand is the number of those who had not bowed the knee to Baal. Then draw the moral: the hour of the witnesses’ triumph is the hour of a retributive warning on the city where they were slain — rejected reformation avenges itself in revolution, and the city which might have been purified by the word is purged by the spirit of judgment; good is effected even through fear, some are saved though as by fire, and unlike those who repented not under the earlier plagues these give glory to the God of heaven, so that the visible Church is stirred and there is a reaction from the spirit of worldliness. Add that a general movement toward Christianity induced by fear or despair is a prediction fulfilled more than once in ecclesiastical history, and that giving glory is a recognition of God’s power. On the fourteenth verse, say the second woe is the sixth trumpet with the two episodes attached, and the third woe is the seventh trumpet which now cometh quickly, a phrase usually pointing to the Parousia. Then decline the survey of opinions: it would be unprofitable, humiliating and discouraging to enumerate all the views that have been held, and the reader may be referred to the collections; report only the opinion of one recent expositor, that a competent number of divinely commissioned and faithful Christian witnesses, endowed with miraculous powers, bore testimony against the corrupt Jews during the last days of their commonwealth, and that the Jews by destroying them brought upon themselves an aggravated and awful doom. And make the structural point that governs the whole: the angel who descended from heaven declared that the end should not be delayed beyond the sounding of the seventh trumpet, so that whatever view is adopted concerning the interpretation of this book must be governed by the plainly declared fact that the seventh trumpet brings us to the very end.

Note that one printed edition and some copies read the same day rather than the same hour, and take the time to be that of the resurrection and ascension of the witnesses, as there was an earthquake at the resurrection of Christ. Understand it of a very great commotion in the civil affairs of kingdoms and nations within the Roman jurisdiction, such as there was when pagan Rome was near its ruin. On the fourteenth verse, say the second woe is past not in the seer’s time except in a visionary way, but that the second woe trumpet, which is the sixth, will have done sounding when the four angels bound in the river have been loosed and have done what they were designed to do, when the two witnesses have been slain and raised and have ascended, and when the things attending thereon — the earthquake, the slaughter and the conversions of men — are accomplished.

Observe that the sounding of the seventh and last trumpet is ushered in by the usual warning and demand of attention, the second woe being past and the third coming quickly; and that this sounding had been suspended for some time, until the apostle had been made acquainted with certain intervening occurrences of very great moment and worthy of his notice, so that what he had before expected he now at last heard. Then set out the effects and consequences of the trumpet when it is sounded, beginning with the loud and joyful acclamations of the saints and angels in heaven, and observing both the manner of their adorations, that they rose from their seats and fell upon their faces and worshipped God with reverence and humility, and the matter of them.

Argue from this verse that the city is not Babylon or Rome but Jerusalem, and call the proof unanswerable: Babylon shall be wholly burned before the fulfilling of the mystery of God, whereas this city is not burned at all, but at the fulfilling of that mystery a tenth part of it is destroyed by an earthquake and the other nine parts converted. Then reckon it out: seven thousand slain, being a tenth part of the inhabitants, who were therefore seventy thousand in all, so that the remaining sixty-three thousand were converted, a grand step toward the fulfilling of the mystery of God — such a conversion as we nowhere else read of, so that there shall be a larger as well as a holier church at Jerusalem than ever was yet. Call the terror blessed, and giving glory the character of true conversion. And mark the change of title: he is styled the Lord of the earth when he declares his right over the earth by the two witnesses, but the God of heaven when he not only gives rain from heaven after the afflicting drought but declares his majesty from heaven by taking his witnesses up into it; and when the whole multitude gives glory to the God of heaven, then that treading of the holy city ceases. Elsewhere take the earthquake for violent commotions among the persecutors and revolutions of states, say many perished in these popular commotions, and have the remnant receive the pure doctrines of the gospel and glorify God for his judgments and their own conversion. And on the woes, either refer all three to the destruction of Jerusalem — the first the seditions among the Jews themselves, the second the besieging of the city by the Romans, the third the taking and sacking of the city and the burning of the temple, the greatest of the three, in which nearly a million of men lost their lives — or else date them: the second woe, the butchery made by the Saracens, ceasing about the year 847 when their power was so broken by Charles the Great that they never recovered it, and the prelude of the third coming while the Roman see enlarged its power and grandeur, until in the year 755 the bishop of Rome became a secular prince by king Pepin’s gift of the exarchate of Lombardy.

debates: Whether the great city of this passage is Jerusalem or Rome.
Whether the numbers ten and seven thousand are proportions or counts.
Whether a conversion produced by terror is a true conversion.
What the three woes correspond to in history.
Whether the seventh trumpet brings the book to its end.
outliers: Wesley calls the tenth part an unanswerable proof that the city is Jerusalem, and computes its population from the death toll.
Ellicott asks whether the seven thousand deliberately answers the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal.
Ellicott sums the verse as rejected reformation avenging itself in revolution.
Barnes refuses to survey the interpretations, calling the attempt humiliating and discouraging.
Clarke and Wesley give incompatible historical schemes for the three woes, one first-century and one medieval.
Wesley dates the second woe to 847 and the prelude of the third to Pepin’s gift of 755.
Ellicott makes the seventh trumpet the fixed point by which every reading of the book must be governed.

15.pericope_label: And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever — and the four and twenty elders, which sat before God on their seats, fell upon their faces, and worshipped God — saying, We give thee thanks, O Lord God Almighty, which art, and wast, and art to come; because thou hast taken to thee thy great power, and hast reigned

schools.summary: Say this is the last of the trumpets, so that under it the series of visions ends and the affairs of the world are wound up; place it where the events pertaining to the colossal Roman power, the fourth kingdom of the prophet, are completed and the reign of the saints begins, that is at the termination of the twelve hundred and sixty years of the papacy, the downfall of that persecuting power being the introduction of the kingdom of God on earth. Then correct the English: it is the kingdom, not the kingdoms, of the world which has become Christ’s possession, since the contest is not for the separate nationalities, whose varying political systems might exist as mere organisations under his rule, but for the kingdom of the world; and supply the word possession or inheritance from the Psalm which foretells this establishment of the kingdom of the anointed. Note that the participle for saying is masculine though the noun for voices is feminine, a construction according to sense; that the aorist is prophetic, treating as already a fact what is foretold; and that God the Father is meant by Lord here, as the following pronoun shows. Then make the drama plain: Satan wields the kingdom of the world which he offered to Christ on the mountain for one act of worship, but Christ scorned partnership with Satan in the rule of the world and chose war, war up to the hilt and to the end, and now the climax has come with him as conqueror of the kingdom of this world for his Father — which is the crowning lesson of this book. On the elders, translate seated upon their thrones, not seats: the word is the same which is rendered throne when it refers to our Lord and seat when it refers to Satan, and it is better rendered throne throughout, since by that variation two great ideas which run through this book are obliterated, the one that the true servants of Christ are crowned with him and share his sovereignty, the other that the antagonism of the prince of darkness to the prince of light develops itself in a parody of the heavenly kingdom. Say the elders represent the Church of God in all ages, seated with Christ in heavenly places even while they toil and sorrow on earth; note that though they have thrones of their own they fall upon their faces in every act of worship, and that they represent the redeemed as the four living creatures represent the forces of nature. On the thanksgiving, note the vocative and nominative forms standing together in the divine title; that the perfect thou hast taken emphasises the permanence of God’s rule, thou hast assumed thy power, while the aorist that follows is ingressive, thou didst begin to reign; and that the same combination of tenses occurs elsewhere without confusion. Take the unchanging name as the pledge that in all the revolutions which occur on the earth God remains the same, and hear the echo of the Second Psalm throughout the chorus, the heathen having raged and their counsel against the Lord and his anointed having come to nought.

Clear away the wrong datings first. The days of the voice of this angel cannot refer to the times of Constantine, for though there was then a strange turn of affairs in favour of the kingdom of Christ, with a great spread of the gospel and large conversions and many churches formed in several countries and the whole empire become Christian, yet this came to pass under the sixth seal, before any of the trumpets were sounded, and much less this seventh and last. Nor do they belong to the times of the Reformation in Germany. One writer fixes the sounding of this trumpet to the year 1558, when the kings of Sweden and Denmark set up the gospel in their kingdoms and reformed them from Popery, and when Queen Elizabeth came to the throne of England and rooted out great part of the Romish superstition; but it is certain that this angel has not yet sounded his trumpet, and therefore it cannot refer to anything past, but to what is to come. Then take the person addressed in the thanksgiving to be the Lord Jesus Christ, whose the kingdoms are become and who now reigns in great power and authority; he is Lord of all, and truly and properly God, and the Almighty, as his works of creation, preservation, redemption and raising himself from the dead declare — and each of these titles suits him exceedingly well when his visible kingdom on earth shall be so greatly enlarged.

Say this trumpet contains the most important and joyful events, and renders all the former trumpets matter of joy to all the inhabitants of heaven, the allusion being to the trumpets used in festal solemnities. Then argue from a contrast: at the opening of the seventh seal there was silence in heaven, and at the sounding of the seventh trumpet great voices — and this alone is sufficient to show that the seven seals and the seven trumpets do not run parallel to each other. Add that as soon as the seventh angel sounds the kingdom falls to God and his Christ, which immediately appears in heaven and is there celebrated with joyful praise, though on earth several dreadful occurrences are to appear first. Take the kingdom of the world as the royal government over the whole world and all its kingdoms: this province has been in the enemy’s hands, and now returns to its rightful Master. On the elders, note that they sit before God on thrones, which we do not read of any angel, and that they shall reign over the earth. On the thanksgiving, observe that God is frequently styled He who is and who was and who is to come, but that now he is actually come the words who is to come are as it were swallowed up, so that to thank him for taking his great power is all one with thanking him that he is come; and say that God has never ceased to use his power, but has suffered his enemies to oppose it, which he will now suffer no more. Elsewhere say the heavenly host, angels and redeemed human spirits together, magnify God that he has discomfited his enemies and rendered his friends glorious; ask when this shall be, and report that some say it has already taken place in the destruction of the Jewish state and the sending of the gospel through the Gentile world, while others refer it to the millennium and the consummation of all things. And say the three tenses of the divine name together give the proper view of God in his eternity, comprehending the present, the past and the future.

debates: When the seventh trumpet sounds, or has sounded.
Whether the text reads the kingdom or the kingdoms of the world.
Whether the elders sit on seats or on thrones.
Whether the seals and the trumpets run parallel to each other.
To whom the thanksgiving is addressed.
outliers: Gill rejects three proposed datings by name and concludes the trumpet has not yet sounded at all.
Barnes fixes the sounding at the end of the twelve hundred and sixty years of the papacy, where Gill refuses to fix it anywhere past.
Ellicott insists on the singular kingdom and distinguishes the nationalities from the world-kingdom at issue.
Robertson makes the refused bargain on the mountain the key to the whole book.
Wesley argues from silence at the seventh seal against great voices at the seventh trumpet that the two series are not parallel.
Ellicott argues that rendering one Greek word two ways destroys two structural ideas of the Apocalypse.
Wesley observes that the clause who is to come has been dropped from the divine title because he has now come.

18.pericope_label: And the nations were angry, and thy wrath is come, and the time of the dead, that they should be judged, and that thou shouldest give reward unto thy servants the prophets, and to the saints, and them that fear thy name, small and great; and shouldest destroy them which destroy the earth — and the temple of God was opened in heaven, and there was seen in his temple the ark of his testament

schools.summary: Take the anger of the nations for the whole series of events preceding the final establishment of the kingdom, the opposition to his laws, the persecution of his people, the slaying of his witnesses, and every attempt to throw off his government; at the moment of triumph it is natural to look back to those darker times when the nations raged and the very existence of the church was in jeopardy. Note the ingressive aorist, they became angry, and call this the culmination of the world’s hostility against Christ. Take the coming of the wrath as a prophetic aorist, the wrath conceived as already come; by the dead understand both good and bad, coincident with the resurrection and the judgment; and note that the reward comes at the end of the day, from God, at the Lord’s return, according to each man’s work, and that the accusative in the small and the great is an anacoluthon which fails to agree with the datives before it, though some manuscripts correct it. On the last verse, say the earthly temple was a pattern of the heavenly, that God dwells in heaven as in a holy temple of which that on earth was the emblem, and that its opening means the seer was permitted to look into the abode of God and see him in his glory, the very interior being laid open with its most hidden mysteries. Argue from this that the verse begins a new series of visions rather than closing this one, since in the first series there is a remarkably similar statement, that a door was opened in heaven so that the seer might look in — which agrees with the judgment that this chapter is improperly divided and should have closed at the previous verse. Or take up the distinction drawn at the first verse between the two words for temple: it is the inner house that is now opened, and opened to its very inmost recesses, for not the holy place alone is disclosed but the holiest of all, the shrine of shrines which the high priest alone entered, and he only once a year, as though the veil had been rent anew — so that, read by the light of the measuring, the secret abode of the safeguarded children of God is revealed. In the hour of apostasy and worldliness the faithful had found their strength in the shadow of the Almighty and were regarded by God as his true living temple; now that the end has come there is no need that they should be hidden any more. On the ark, note it stood within the second veil of the tabernacle and in the inner chamber of the first temple, and probably perished when that temple was burnt.

Take the anger of the nations to refer not to the times of the dragon or the pagan emperors, who were wroth with the woman and made war with her seed, but to papal Rome and its Gentiles, the nations over which antichrist reigns. And do not make it their anger against Christ and his people, expressed by anathemas, excommunications, murders and bloody persecutions, since these could not be matter of thanksgiving to the elders; make it rather their anger and resentment at his power and reign, at having the outward court taken from them which was said to be given them, and at their loss of power, profit, pleasure and plenty through the fall of Babylon and the setting up of Christ’s kingdom — things which will make the followers of antichrist gnash their teeth while they occasion joy and thanksgiving among the saints. On the last verse, take the allusion from the temple at Jerusalem, which was the place of public worship, was shut up in times of idolatry and fell to decay, and had its doors opened and repaired whenever there was a reformation. The sense is that the pure worship of God will now be restored and freely exercised, the temple open to all, where everyone may come and sit and worship without fear; churches will be formed according to the original plan and primitive order, the laws of Christ concerning the admission, regulation and exclusion of members punctually observed, and the ordinances kept as they were first delivered and purged of all the corruptions introduced by Papists or retained by Protestants — the Lord’s supper freed from the senseless notions of transubstantiation and consubstantiation and from all the vain ceremonies that attend it, and baptism administered as it was at first.

Say the wrath of the heathen now rises to its highest pitch, but meets the wrath of the Almighty and melts away, and that the verse describes both the going forth and the end of God’s wrath, which together take up several ages. Take the time of the dead to include both the quick and the dead, of whom those already dead are far the more numerous part; and since the judgment is infallibly certain, let it be spoken of as already present. Grade the rewards: to his servants the prophets, to his saints, to them who were eminently holy, and then to them that fear his name, who are the lowest class — for those who do not even fear God will have no reward from him; and add that the reward is of free grace, not of debt, and that small and great means all universally, young and old, high and low, rich and poor. Then expand the destroying of the earth: it was destroyed by the great whore in particular, but likewise in general by the open rage and hate of wicked men against all that is good, by wars and the destruction and desolation naturally flowing from them, and by such laws and constitutions as hinder much good and occasion many offences and calamities. Elsewhere read the judging as avenging, the word being often so used, and take the dead to mean those slain for the testimony of Jesus. On the last verse, say the true worship of God was established in the Christian Church, which is the true temple, that at Jerusalem being destroyed; note that the ark made by Moses was not in the second temple, being probably burnt with the first, so that this is the heavenly ark of the everlasting covenant of which the other was the shadow, seen now as a testimony that what God has promised shall be fulfilled to the uttermost; and observe that the lightnings, voices, thunders, earthquake and great hail occur again in the very same order when the seventh angel pours out his vial, so that one place answers the other, and what the trumpet here denounces in heaven is there executed by the vial upon earth. And confess plainly that you have come to a part of this book deemed of the greatest importance by the Protestant Church but peculiarly difficult and obscure, that you have often acknowledged your own incapacity to illustrate these prophecies, and that you might have availed yourself of the labours of others but do not know who is right, or whether any writer on the book has hit the sense.

debates: What the anger of the nations is directed at.
Whether the dead to be judged are the martyrs or all men.
Whether the last verse closes this chapter or opens the next series.
Which ark is seen in the opened temple.
Whether the rewards named form a descending scale.
outliers: Clarke confesses his incapacity to interpret what follows and defers to another author whose views he will not endorse — his fourth refusal in this chapter.
Gill rejects the persecution reading of the nations’ anger on the ground that massacres could not be matter of thanksgiving.
Barnes argues from a parallel in the first series that this verse begins a new vision, and that the chapter is wrongly divided.
Wesley matches the five signs here, in order, with the same five at the seventh vial, and reads one as the execution of the other.
Wesley grades the rewards and concludes that those who do not even fear God receive none.
Ellicott reads the opened sanctuary as the disclosure of the hidden people of God, taking up his own distinction from the first verse.
Gill turns the opened temple into a programme of church reform aimed at Protestants as well as Papists.
